圖姆比琴主要出現在旁遮普民間音樂與西方巴恩格拉音樂中，也見於旁遮普蘇菲歌手的演唱: The tumbi appears mainly in Punjabi folk music and in Western bhangra music, and also on occasions when Punjabi Sufi singers perform; in Western mainstream pop and hip-hop its high single-string plucking can be heard, for example on Missy Elliott's 〈Get Ur Freak On〉, Panjabi MC's 〈Mundian Ton Bach Ke Rahin〉, Master P's 〈20 Inch〉 and 〈Baby Doll〉.
圖姆比琴以其清亮、尖銳的音色著稱，具有鮮明的穿透力。單弦設計賦予其高音域的特性，: The tumbi is known for its clear, sharp timbre, with a marked penetration. Its single-string design gives it a high register, and its tone is bright and strongly regional. Its timbre has both a metallic edge and a woody warmth: it does not lose the plainness of a traditional instrument, yet it sounds modern.
圖姆比琴是印度次大陸北部旁遮普地區的傳統單弦撥奏樂器，與旁遮普民間音樂相連，現亦: The tumbi is a traditional single-string plucked instrument of the Punjab in the north of the Indian subcontinent, tied to Punjabi folk music and now also common in Western bhangra. In modern times it was promoted by Lal Chand Yamla Jatt; in the 1960s to 1980s it was taken up by singers such as Kuldip Manak, Muhammad Sadiq, Didar Sandhu and Amar Singh Chamkila, and the Sufi singer Sain Zahoor also used it. It then entered Western pop music, and in 2001 Missy Elliott's single 〈Get Ur Freak On〉 and Panjabi MC's 〈Mundian Ton Bach Ke Rahin〉 brought its sound into the mainstream.

圖姆比琴（Tumbi，旁遮普語 ਤੂੰਬੀ，亦稱 tumba/toomba）是南: The tumbi (Punjabi ਤੂੰਬੀ, also called tumba/toomba) is a traditional chordophone of the Punjab in South Asia, a wooden stick fitted with a gourd-shell resonator, with a single metal string crossing the bridge on the resonator and tied to a tuning peg at the end of the stick. The player sounds it by plucking and flicking the string repeatedly with the index finger, and its tone is high. It is common in Punjabi folk music and used by Sufi singers, and is now also found in Western bhangra.
在共鳴方面，圖姆比琴通過木製共鳴箱與弦的振動相互作用，產生具有特殊韻味的持續音。: As for resonance, the tumbi uses the interaction of the wooden soundbox with the vibration of the string to produce a sustained note with a flavour of its own. Beside the violin its timbre is more direct and sharp; beside the guzheng it lacks the deep, far-reaching quality, but is lighter and more active. Its sound is instantly recognisable in Punjabi folk song, and in a bhangra arrangement especially it catches the listener's ear at once and becomes an important carrier of the melody.
